Inherited from Old Church Slavonic абиѥ (abije, “now, immediately”), from Proto-Slavic *abьje.

From Old Church Slavonic агарѣнинъ (agarěninŭ), from Ancient Greek ἀγαρηνός (agarēnós), derived from Hagar, canonically the mother of Ishmael in the Bible.

From Old Church Slavonic алчьба (alčĭba, “hunger, thirst”), from Proto-Slavic *оlčьba, *alьčьba. Morphologically equivalent to а́лчен (álčen, “greedy”) + -ба (-ba).

parole.significato: boulder, block (a large, heavy, roughly shaped stone or cuboid)

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic блазнити (blazniti), from Proto-Slavic *blazniti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleǵ- (“to strike”).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic бобръ (bobrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bobrъ.

parole.significato: god → the God (in monotheism) / male deity (in polytheism)

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic болѣти (bolěti).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic брашьно (brašĭno), from Proto-Slavic *boršьno.

parole.significato: to see (to have the power of sight)

parole.significato: You; the second-person plural pronoun in the nominative case, used as the subject of a verb.

parole.significato: guilt, blame (property or emotion of being guilty)

parole.significato: rope, line, cord, cable, hawser, lanyard

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic възбоуждати (vŭzbuždati).
From въз- (văz-, “ex-, out-”) + кли́кна (klíkna, “shout, beckon”), from Old Church Slavonic кликати (klikati), кличѫ (kličǫ).

parole.significato: to fall in love with, to grow fond of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic възлюбити (vŭzljubiti). By surface analysis, въз- (văz-) + лю́бя (ljúbja).

parole.significato: wolf (Canis lupus; the largest wild member of the canine subfamily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic влькъ (vlĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьlkъ.

parole.significato: wool (fur of sheep, goats, and other Ungulata)

parole.significato: outside (not within the confines of a place or enclosed space)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic вънъ (vŭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъnъ.

parole.significato: to embody, to incarnate, to personify
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic въплътити (vŭplŭtiti). By surface analysis, въ- (vă-) + плът (plăt, “flesh”) + -я (-ja).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic вѣра (věra), from Proto-Slavic *věra.

parole.significato: to believe (to feel certain that something is true or that somebody is telling the truth)

parole.significato: death, especially when premature or unnatural

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic гробъ (grobŭ), from Proto-Slavic *grobъ.

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic коньчина (konĭčina), from Proto-Slavic *konьčina.

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic фараѡнъ (faraonŭ), borrowed from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew פַּרְעֹה, borrowed from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“palace, pharaoh”, literally “pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“great, big”)”).
From Old Church Slavonic хвальба (xvalĭba), from Proto-Slavic *xvalьba. Morphologically equivalent to хва́ла (hvála, “praise”) + -ба (-ba).

parole.significato: to praise, to commend, to compliment
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хвалити (xvaliti), from Proto-Slavic *xvaliti.
Derived from Old Church Slavonic хꙑзъ (xyzŭ), of Germanic origin. Cognate with English house.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хꙑтрость (xytrostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *xytrostь. Equivalent to хи́тър (hítăr, “cunning, clever”) + -ост (-ost).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хꙑтръ (xytrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хлѣбъ (xlěbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xlěbъ, from a Germanic language, likely Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃 (hlaifs).

parole.significato: church banner, gonfalon (a religious banner with images of saints, typically carried in processions on major Christian…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хорѫгꙑ (xorǫgy), from Proto-Slavic *xorǫgy.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic храбръ (xrabrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xorbrъ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic храмъ (xramŭ, “home, temple”), from Proto-Slavic *xormъ (“wooden building”).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хѫдожьство (xǫdožĭstvo).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хѫдожьникъ (xǫdožĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xǫdogъ (from a reflex of Proto-Germanic *handugaz).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic цѣсарь (cěsarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic цвѣтъ (cvětŭ), from Proto-Slavic *květъ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic цѣльба (cělĭba). By surface analysis, цял (cjal) + -ба (-ba).

parole.significato: soundness of mind and soul, prudence, chastity
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic цѣломѫдрьѥ (cělomǫdrĭje), а Calque of Ancient Greek σωφροσύνη (sōphrosúnē). Formed as цял (cjal, “whole”) + -о- (-o-) + мъ́дър (mắdăr, “wise”) + -ие (-ie).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic цѣна (cěna), from Proto-Slavic *cěna.

parole.significato: entire, whole, all (the), full, intact, in one piece, complete, completed, unabridged
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic цѣлъ (cělŭ), from Proto-Slavic *cě̑lъ.
From Old Church Slavonic чародѣи (čaroděi), from Proto-Slavic *čarodějь.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чаша (čaša), from Proto-Slavic *čaša.

parole.significato: forehead (the part of the face above the eyebrows and below the hairline)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чело (čelo), from Proto-Slavic *čelo, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₃os.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чрьвенъ (črĭvenŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьrvenъ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чрьнъ (črĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьrnъ.

parole.significato: to draw, to scoop (water with a vessel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чрьпати (črĭpati), from Proto-Slavic *čьrpati.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чьсть (čĭstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь.

parole.significato: to read (to look at and understand written or printed text)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чьсти (čĭsti), from Proto-Slavic *čisti. Doublet of чи́там (čítam).

parole.significato: Thursday (the fifth day of the week in many religious traditions, and the fourth day of the week in systems using the I…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic четврьтъкъ (četvrĭtŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъkъ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic четꙑре (četyre), from Proto-Slavic *četyre, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чии (čii), from Proto-Slavic *čьjь.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic число (čislo), from Proto-Slavic *čislo. Morphologically formed as чи́там (čítam, “to account, to esteem”) + -сло (-slo).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чловѣкъ (člověkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьlověkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kelawaikas, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чловѣчьскъ (člověčĭskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čelověčьskъ. By surface analysis, чове́к (čovék) + -шки (-ški).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чоудимъ (čudimŭ), a fossilized present passive participle of чу́дя се (čúdja se, “to wonder”) + -им (-im).

parole.significato: wonderworker, thaumaturge - one who performs miracles (epithet of a saint)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чоудотворьць (čudotvorĭcĭ), itself a calque of Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós). By surface analysis, чу́до (čúdo) + -о- (-o-) + творе́ц (tvoréc). Compare Russian чудотворец (čudotvorec) and Serbo-Croatian чудотворац.
Possibly from Old Church Slavonic чешоуꙗ (češuja).
From Old Church Slavonic шаръ (šarŭ), probably of Oghur origin, related to the adjective Proto-Turkic *siarïg (“bright, yellow”). Akin to the first element in the name of the Šaraghur tribe.
From Old Church Slavonic шатьръ (šatĭrŭ), of Bulgar origin. Cognate with Turkish çadır (“umbrella”), Persian چادر (čâdar, “tent, umbrella”), ultimately from Sanskrit छत्त्र (chattra, “shelter”).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic шесть (šestĭ), from Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. The “best” sense is derived from the Bulgarian schooling system's 2-6 grade scale, where a 6 is the best possible grade.
From Old Church Slavonic шьствие (šĭstvije), шьствьѥ (šĭstvĭje), from Proto-Slavic *šьstvьje. By surface analysis, *шед- (*šed-, suppletive aorist stem of и́да (ída, “to come”)) + -ствие (-stvie).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic широкъ (širokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *širokъ.
From Old Church Slavonic школа (škola), ultimately from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic хътѣти (xŭtěti), from Proto-Slavic *xъtěti.

parole.significato: generous (willing to give and share unsparingly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic щедръ (štedrŭ), штедръ (štedrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ščedrъ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чьто (čĭto), from Proto-Slavic *čьto.

parole.significato: A curb (driving bit for a horse).
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic оузда (uzda), from Proto-Slavic *uzda.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic юница (junica), from Proto-Slavic *junъ (“young”); compare Proto-Slavic *junę (“calf”).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic юность (junostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *junostь.
From Old Church Slavonic юноша (junoša), from Proto-Slavic *junoša.

parole.significato: short form of the third-person singular feminine pronoun in the accusative case, used as the direct object of a verb, t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ѭ (jǫ), from Proto-Slavic *jeję̇.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic авити (aviti), from Proto-Slavic *aviti.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic агода (agoda), from Proto-Slavic *agoda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ṓˀgāˀ.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ꙗдъ (jadŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ědъ (“poison”).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ꙗдениѥ (jadenije).
From Old Church Slavonic ꙗдьца (jadĭca), formed from я́да (jáda, “to eat”) + -ца (-ca).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic аице (aice), from Proto-Slavic *ājьcè.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ꙗсти (jasti), from Proto-Slavic *ě̀sti.

parole.significato: Yat: a former letter of the Bulgarian alphabet, representing a sound between [æ] and [ɛ] and written as Ѣ/ѣ.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ѣть (jětĭ).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic -ачь (-ačĭ) and -чь (-čĭ).

parole.significato: Forms masculine nouns denoting a person associated with a field of study, profession, or characteristic.
parole.testo: For native terms, inherited from Old Church Slavonic -икъ (-ikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ikъ. parole.significato: Forms diminutives of feminine nouns, including personal names
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic -ъка (-ŭka) and -ька (-ĭka) (the latter causes palatalization of preceding velars).

parole.significato: Used to form compound words. Usually excrescent.
parole.testo: For native terms, inherited from Old Church Slavonic -о- (-o-), from Proto-Slavic *-o-. Etymology tree Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. Bulgarian -о- For borrowings, borrowed from Latin -o-, from Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ватахъ (vataxŭ, “chief, commander”). Probably of Oghur origin, related to dialectal Bulgarian ватог (vatog, “hearth”). Alternatively, according to Vl. Georgiev (BER): a Thracian borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to lead”).

parole.significato: a type of jug or pitcher (an instrument for drinking)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic кръчагъ (krŭčagŭ), of disputed origin: * Possibly a native derivation, from къ́ркам (kắrkam, “to swill”) + -аг (-ag). Favoured by Mladenov. * Alternatively, of Oghur origin akin to Hungarian korsó (“jug”). Borrowed into Albanian kërçak.

parole.significato: mother (a female parent, especially of a human; a female who parents a child (which she has given birth to, adopted, fo…
parole.testo: Either as a diminutive form of Proto-Slavic *mati through Old Church Slavonic мати (mati) or from the unattested form in Proto-Slavic *matьka, which through anticipation of the palatalization became the Proto-Slavic *majtka and later through assimilation the /t/ was dropped.

parole.significato: short church service to offer prayer, give thanks or mark a special occasion
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian моле́бен (molében), or from Old Church Slavonic мольбьнъ (molĭbĭnŭ).

Continues Old Church Slavonic соуръ (surŭ), probably of Oghur or Kipchak (Cuman) origin cognate with Kazakh сұр (sur, “gray”) (possibly from Proto-Turkic *sǖr- (“to vade away”)) or from an o-grade of Proto-Slavic *syrъ (“raw, damp”).
